title: Parametric Resonance — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Parametric Resonance's rich face: three walks, the swing, the threshold heard and the pump's phase, each opening on one idea and ending on the page's own claim, and the fingerprint of the words each was made against. Two of them found the swing's timing backwards in the text; that waits as an offer, not an edit. I grow when the entry is enriched again; I never hold the entry's words.

pieces.file: Parametric Resonance — rich — the pumped swing.html
pieces.title: the pumped swing, timed both ways
pieces.caption: **The swing, walked up to its timing.** The swing alone (one swing every 2.84 s at 2 m); standing and squatting once per swing (× 0.986, the same as holding still) and twice (× 1.316 a swing); the page's rule in the page's own equation, θ̈ = −(g⁄L) sin θ, where it builds (× 1.084); and last the same rule on a real swing, where the child's own rising and sinking counts. There it brakes (× 0.743), and the reverse, stand up through the bottom and squat at the ends, builds. The child's work each swing has the same sign as the energy the swing gains. The checks beside it re-run every number.
pieces.near: Each squat-stand changes the swing's effective length

pieces.file: Parametric Resonance — rich — the threshold heard.html
pieces.title: the threshold, heard
pieces.caption: **Decay, then the crack.** A 220 Hz resonator pumped at 440 Hz: one ring alone (fades 18.0 dB a second); a pump below threshold, which only slows the fade (9.0 dB a second at ε = 0.003, as the Floquet multipliers predict); a pump held or swept past ε<sub>c</sub> = 4ζ, where a noise floor 80 dB down grows into a steady tone, and heavier damping moves the threshold; and last the page's open question set up as a test, a driven ring swept into resonance beside a pumped one swept through threshold. The driven one is heard from the start. The pumped one crosses ε<sub>c</sub> at 1.5 s and says nothing until 3.1 s. The multipliers cross 1 at exactly 4ζ for both dampings.
pieces.near: the system's natural damping eats energy faster

pieces.file: Parametric Resonance — rich — with the ring, against it.html
pieces.title: with the ring, against it
pieces.caption: **The two Floquet modes, drawn and heard.** The ring watched once per cycle on the pump's clock, so its phase stands still; the pump switched on at twice the rate, where two lines appear, the eigenvectors of one pump period, and every starting phase ends on the growing one; the pump at the wrong rate, where no growing line exists; and last the section's own test. Struck exactly on the fading line the ring falls at 72 dB a second, four times faster than with no pump, turns at 0.76 s, and is full at 2.37 s; struck on the growing line it is full at 0.11 s. A noisier room turns it sooner.
pieces.near: The stability diagram is phase-blind on purpose

offers.what: The rule "squat at the bottom of the arc, stand at the peaks" brakes a real swing; its reverse builds. Measured in the swing piece (point-mass child, L = 2 m ± 6%, timed by the swing's own phase): the page's rule × 0.743 a swing, the reverse × 1.316, holding still × 0.986. The page's rule builds only in θ̈ = −(g⁄L) sin θ, where length sets only the pitch (× 1.084; reverse × 0.897). Why: in arc length u = Lθ a real swing obeys ü + ((g − L̈)⁄L)u = 0, so the child's own acceleration pumps four times as hard as g⁄L and the other way round; net ε_eff = −3δ (measured −2.99). Proposed: "stand up as you pass through the bottom, squat as you reach the peaks", and a line saying the g⁄L Mathieu reading gets a swing's timing backwards. The same rule is repeated in the first paragraph of Where the phase lives.

The swing paragraph's accounting describes the braking cycle and gives it the wrong sign. Climbing where the rope pulls least (the peaks) and sinking where it pulls most (the bottom) means the swing does more work on the child than the child does on it: over the third swing, the child's work −0.91 J and the swing's energy −0.96 J (30 kg child). The cycle that builds is the reverse, standing against the hardest pull at the bottom and sinking against the softest at the ends: +48.0 J of work, +45.5 J to the swing, the air taking the rest. "Net work done by the child per cycle is positive, and it equals the energy the swing gains" is true of that reversed rule, less the air.

The pumped equation has no damping term, but the sentences after it say amplitude grows "above a threshold ε" and that below it "damping wins". With no damping the threshold at Ω = 2ω₀ is ε = 0. Proposed: write it ẍ + 2ζω₀ẋ + ω₀²(1 + ε cos Ωt)x = 0 and name ε_c ≈ 4ζ at Ω = 2ω₀; The threshold section could carry the same formula beside "less damped systems threshold easier". Measured: the Floquet multipliers cross 1 at ε = 0.006000 for ζ = 0.0015 and at 0.024000 for ζ = 0.006.

"If you pump at the wrong phase you brake the swing instead of building it" holds while the pumper keeps the wrong timing against the swing, as a child does (the swing piece: × 0.743 a swing). Against a fixed pump clock the wrong phase only delays, as the second bullet says: struck exactly on the decaying mode at ε = 3ε_c the ring falls at −72.0 dB/s (Floquet −72.0, no pump −18.0), turns at 0.76 s at −63 dB, and is full at 2.37 s, against 0.11 s on the growing mode; with a noise floor 20 dB higher it turns at 0.59 s and is full at 1.80 s. Proposed: one sentence naming the two cases, a pumper who follows the swing and a pump on its own clock.

The first open question can carry numbers now. Same resonator, same six-second sweeps from the same quiet: the driven ring is above −60 dB from 0.01 s and rises 10→90% in 1.39 s; the pumped one crosses ε_c at 1.50 s, stays under −60 dB until 3.12 s, then rises 10→90% in 0.79 s. The silence comes after the threshold, not at it: the crack lags the crossing by about ln(heard level ⁄ noise floor) ⁄ growth rate. Whether the ear hears it as a crack is still open; no listening was done.
